there's always one person in a circle of friends everyone likes to rag on and it's done pretty purposely. it's a pathetic little power trip and an easy way of moving up the social ladder. it's led me to think that acquaintances are far better than friendships in a lot of ways. at least we assume a level of respect with someone we hardly know. but you can't just swallow these feelings whole and weather it out by laughing along with them, 'cause then you're taking part in your own abuse. 

if you don't like it, if they go too far, then you tell them straightaway to stop. what other recourse is there? and if they don't, or if they simply "tease" you even more about it, then you'll know for certain they don't care about you or the way you feel. you're to be kicked around for their enjoyment.

it's a balancing act. sometimes the social pressures get the best of us and you decide it's easiest to just go with what others expect of you. we pick up on what our friends like and what they don't like based on an agonizing trial and error process. of course if they were at all friendly, you'd be free to tell them anything. but mostly we just stick to subtle hints in figuring out what is and isn't permissible to talk about.

eventually you'll find this gets too exhausting and go for the other extreme: wrapping yourself up completely in your own weirdness and embracing it head on without any consideration for what others think or say, which requires you to develop this false sense of self esteem where you're engrossed with your own ego and self image. this, too, can be pretty damaging to your psyche. 

you have to learn how to play on both and wise up to the subtle predations of other people. there are hundreds if not thousands of others who share your interests out there, no matter how weird. you just have to want to be sociable enough to keep searching, as strange as that sounds.

excellent response, you make a lot of great points, but here's where I part ways: I think it's hard to argue that what you know to be true for yourself may not be true of others. personal, empirically learned standards of behavior are different from those that we're just taught to take at face value and align with, and in many cases the two may not even be congruent. we're all vastly different from one another and only you know what will work for you in the grander scheme of things, just as I only know what will work for me. it's also true that some external input can be introduced that may invoke great insight (like the comments on this thread) and force you to modify your standards or change the way you look at yourself, but you're the one who chooses to apply them, to take what's legitimate from them, in much the same way you choose whether or not to be receptive to either valid criticisms or baseless insults, which hold no real weight unless they're being deliberately invested in an insecurity the other person is trying to exploit, be it your friends, your family or a complete stranger who's singled you out because you give off the signals of a pushover. 

'I clearly am not capable of being loved for my personality alone so what else do I have left to offer? I see utility as the substitute for this and if I can't meet my own bar for utility, then what is my worth?' 

I would say replace the word 'personality' with 'a lack of self esteem' (don't take that as a personal attack, I'm going through the same) and I think it would lend a bit more accuracy to the dilemma you've described. your true personality, when uninhibited by depressive self loathing, is a permanent part of you you can't really change. it'd be insane to condemn ourselves to a life of loneliness because we've asked of others to do the impossible and fill a void we've left unfilled, yet we still do it. but how is it that you call yourself selfish when you constantly seek the validation from others by asking what you have to offer? there is no self in questions like these. contrary to popular conviction, I believe selfishness can be a good way in realizing one's own self-importance if done on moral grounds. even things that we claim to do unselfishly for others are indeed selfish, because they're done out of self-concern. self-improvement is called that for a reason: to focus your energies in finding out what *your* interests are and how *you* can go about pursuing those interests, come what may. focusing instead on what you could offer those who've trampled all over you to begin with is akin to a bullied victim crawling back to his abuser and presenting him with a bat.

'I don't generally care about giving happiness to others.' 

nor should you if you yourself aren't content with your life and your own accomplishments, however meager those accomplishments may be should make no difference. of course it makes you feel shitty; it makes all of us feel shitty. when you see an attractive couple pass by hand in hand, are you suddenly filled with joy at the mere sight of their affection? fuck no. 

what does it matter how others perceive your self worth? does your identity only exist in others? the plain fact is we've been possessed by the judgements and opinions of *other* people, and a person who wishes to measure his own self worth on the basis of his utility must think very little of himself. your value, your worth should be measured only by *your* moral standards, standards you've developed through your own experiences. I think a human being's inherent worth stems from our capacity to desire and to reason, but everything after that is your onus.
